In general I think it's important to simply realize that today all mainstream media sites today are struggling. Here's an excellent article on the state of the media from a 50 year veteran editor/journalist for the Washington Post. The hey-day for catch-all centralized media outlets is simply gone. Most would have long since gone out of business if not for the fact they tend to be owned by much larger companies. Comcast owns NBC, Time Warner owns CNN, Disney owns ABC, and so on.

What you're left with is companies in desperation. That leads to appeals to bias and click bait. Real news is not interesting. It's up to the user to come to their own conclusion after carefully analyzing the reporter's painstaking efforts to prevent as clear and objective picture as possible. And that happens in a world where articles like that get 1/5000th as much traffic as some clickbait site's "TOP 7 THINGS YOU DIDN'T KNOW ABOUT [______]" which the author threw together on his lunch break.

The dangerous thing about what's happened to the media today is that we're all biased. When you find a news organization saying things that appeal to you in a reasonably eloquent fashion, it's so so easy to suddenly think you've found the bastion of sanity in the media. It can be tough to take a step back and realize how absurd it all is.

I find a decent idea here is to clean your cache/cookies and then visit a site's front page. Most browsers' incognito/anonymous/porn modes will do this naturally. This will generally give you a good idea of the site's agenda since they're going to put out the generic headlines that most match their agenda and the demographic they're trying to appeal to. You can also learn a lot about a site by the way they phrase headlines on controversial topics. Somebody mentioned The Independent. Their phrasing for the headline of the recent police shooting was, "White police officer killed fleeing black man 'like a deer running through the woods.'" The BBC did an interview with Lance Armstrong and asked him, if he were put in the exact same situation again, would he cheat again. He explained that in modern times he certainly wouldn't because it wouldn't be necessary but if he were warped back to 1995 when it was completely and totally pervasive that he probably would. They ran the interview under the headline, "I'd probably cheat again - Armstrong". That links to the transcript of the interview with Lance. Look at links at the bottom to see the hyperlink phrasing - which was also used on their front page.

So to answer your question - there is no single "good" source anymore. Caveat emptor.

These are good ideas. I will be using the cache clearing method you mentioned more frequently in my news consumption.
